SECTION 2556 OMITTED OR UNADJUDICATED COMMUNITY PROPERTY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

DECLARATION OF PARTIES AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Family Code Section 2556 Omitted or Unadjudicated Community Property Information Sheet concerns Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, whose marital dissolution, nullity of marriage, or legal separation proceeding is pending, has concluded by judgment, or may be filed, in the California superior court for Sacramento County. It describes what California law says about a community estate asset or liability that was not addressed, or not fully addressed, by a judgment in such a proceeding — sometimes called an "omitted asset." It states, in general terms, the court's continuing jurisdiction over such items under Family Code section 2556, the procedural mechanism the statute provides, the equal-division standard the statute applies, how published California decisions have described what counts as "omitted or not adjudicated," and the historical background of this area of law. This information sheet does not determine, calculate, or assert that any particular asset or liability connected to Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee was, or was not, adjudicated by any judgment in their case, whether any statutory ground supports an unequal division of such an item, or whether an express written agreement between them addresses the point; those are matters for the court to decide based on the specific facts and the language of the specific judgment, or for Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee to resolve by their own written agreement.

WHAT “COMMUNITY ESTATE” MEANS FOR PURPOSES OF THIS STATUTE — FAMILY CODE SECTION 63
Family Code section 2556, addressed in this document's companion clauses, uses the term “community estate” to describe the assets and liabilities over which it grants the court continuing jurisdiction. Family Code section 63 defines that term for purposes of the Family Code generally: “community estate” includes both community property and quasi-community property. This means that, by this separate definitional section, section 2556's continuing jurisdiction is not limited to community property in the narrower sense; it extends to quasi-community property as well, because quasi-community property falls within the defined term “community estate” that section 2556 itself uses.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "“Community estate” includes both community property and quasi-community property."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 63 (California Legislative Information text), the statutory definition of “community estate” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=63.)
  Known gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 63, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. Section 2556's own text does not use the phrase “quasi-community property” anywhere within it; the conclusion that section 2556 reaches quasi-community property rests on this separate general definition in section 63 (added by the same 1993 enactment that amended section 2556) rather than on any language internal to section 2556 itself. This document does not restate the separate definition of “quasi-community property” found in Family Code section 125, nor does it address how a party establishes, as an evidentiary matter, that a particular asset acquired outside California would have been community property had the acquiring spouse been domiciled in California — the substantive test section 125 states for quasi-community property. This clause also does not address the narrower statutory definition of “community property” itself, which appears elsewhere in the Family Code and is not restated here.

CONTINUING JURISDICTION OVER COMMUNITY ESTATE ASSETS AND LIABILITIES NOT PREVIOUSLY ADJUDICATED — FAMILY CODE SECTION 2556
Family Code section 2556 states that, in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, for nullity of marriage, or for legal separation of the parties, the court has continuing jurisdiction to award community estate assets or community estate liabilities to the parties that have not been previously adjudicated by a judgment in the proceeding. By its own terms, this continuing jurisdiction attaches specifically to the three listed proceeding types and specifically to community estate assets or liabilities — as opposed to, for example, separate property, or matters such as child or spousal support that are governed by their own separate statutory frameworks.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "In a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, for nullity of marriage, or for legal separation of the parties, the court has continuing jurisdiction to award community estate assets or community estate liabilities to the parties that have not been previously adjudicated by a judgment in the proceeding."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2556 (California Legislative Information text), the continuing-jurisdiction grant over previously unadjudicated community estate assets and liabilities (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2556.)
  Known gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 2556's first sentence, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. The statute's own text does not itself define “previously adjudicated,” and California Court of Appeal decisions interpreting that phrase are addressed in this document's separate companion clause on what counts as omitted or not adjudicated — that companion clause states a judicial interpretation, not the statute's own text, and this clause does not restate it. This clause also does not address whether, or how, section 2556's continuing jurisdiction interacts with a party's separate property claims, with support orders, with a summary dissolution proceeding, or with a nonmarital relationship such as a Marvin action, all of which are addressed, if at all, by separate authorities outside this document. Section 2556 is part of Family Code Division 7 (Division of Property), Part 2 (General Provisions), sections 2550 through 2556; this clause does not restate or analyze section 2550's general equal-division rule for the community estate as a whole, which is addressed separately in this document's companion clause on the equal-division standard only insofar as it distinguishes that rule from section 2556's own good-cause standard for omitted items.

HOW ADJUDICATION IS OBTAINED: POSTJUDGMENT MOTION OR ORDER TO SHOW CAUSE IN THE SAME PROCEEDING — FAMILY CODE SECTION 2556
Family Code section 2556 states that a party may file a postjudgment motion or order to show cause in the proceeding in order to obtain adjudication of any community estate asset or liability omitted or not adjudicated by the judgment. By its own terms, this provision identifies the procedural vehicle — a postjudgment motion or order to show cause filed in the same family law proceeding, rather than a separate lawsuit — available for that adjudication.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "A party may file a postjudgment motion or order to show cause in the proceeding in order to obtain adjudication of any community estate asset or liability omitted or not adjudicated by the judgment."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2556 (California Legislative Information text), the postjudgment motion or order to show cause mechanism (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2556.)
  Known gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 2556's second sentence, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. This citation is to the same statutory section, 2556, cited by this document's other authority clauses; they are not independent of one another. The statute's own text does not itself state a filing deadline or statute of limitations for this postjudgment motion or order to show cause, does not itself state what showing a moving party must make to establish that a particular asset or liability was in fact omitted or not adjudicated (a question this document's separate companion clause addresses only insofar as published decisions have described a general standard, not as it would apply to any specific asset), and does not address what happens procedurally if the original case file is no longer available under the applicable court records retention schedule. This clause also does not address whether a different procedural vehicle, such as a separate civil action, remains available or necessary in any particular circumstance; this document's companion clause on historical background addresses only how the law in this area has changed over time in general terms.

THE EQUAL-DIVISION DEFAULT AND THE GOOD-CAUSE EXCEPTION — FAMILY CODE SECTION 2556
Family Code section 2556 states that in these cases — that is, cases in which a party has filed a postjudgment motion or order to show cause to obtain adjudication of an omitted or unadjudicated community estate asset or liability — the court shall equally divide the omitted or unadjudicated community estate asset or liability, unless the court finds upon good cause shown that the interests of justice require an unequal division of the asset or liability. By its own terms, the statute states equal division as the default outcome and permits an unequal division only upon a good-cause finding tied to the interests of justice.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "In these cases, the court shall equally divide the omitted or unadjudicated community estate asset or liability, unless the court finds upon good cause shown that the interests of justice require an unequal division of the asset or liability."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2556 (California Legislative Information text), the equal-division default and the good-cause exception for an unequal division (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2556.)
  Known gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 2556's third sentence, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. This citation is to the same statutory section, 2556, cited by this document's other authority clauses; they are not independent of one another. The statute's own text does not itself define “good cause” or list factors relevant to “the interests of justice” for this purpose; that determination is a matter for the court based on the specific facts. This standard is textually distinct from Family Code section 2550's general rule for dividing the community estate as a whole, which permits an unequal division whenever the parties themselves agree to it in writing or by oral stipulation in open court, without requiring any court finding of good cause; section 2556, by contrast, requires an affirmative good-cause finding by the court for an unequal division of an omitted or unadjudicated item even where the statute's own text does not on its face condition that standard on the absence of a party agreement. This document does not analyze how those two distinct provisions apply together, or address whether a party agreement concerning an omitted asset would be treated under section 2556's good-cause standard, section 2550's agreement-based exception, or some other authority; that is a matter for the court.

WHAT COUNTS AS “OMITTED OR NOT ADJUDICATED”: THE ACTUALLY-LITIGATED-AND-DIVIDED STANDARD
California's Sixth District Court of Appeal has addressed how to determine whether a particular community estate item was, or was not, previously adjudicated for purposes of Family Code section 2556. In Thorne v. Raccina, the court explained that the mere mention of an asset in the judgment is not controlling, and that, quoting an earlier appellate decision, the crucial question is whether the benefits were actually litigated and divided in the previous proceeding. Applying that standard, the court held that a pension the original judgment expressly and unambiguously divided by a fixed formula — even where a party later asserted the formula understated her community interest — was not an omitted asset within the meaning of section 2556, distinguishing it from a separate case in which only a portion of a pension had actually been divided by the original judgment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "The mere mention of an asset in the judgment is not controlling."
  — Thorne v. Raccina, 203 Cal.App.4th 492, 501 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810875/thorne-v-raccina/)
  "crucial question is whether the benefits were actually litigated and divided in the previous proceeding."
  — Thorne v. Raccina, 203 Cal.App.4th 492, 501, quoting Miller v. Miller (1981) 117 Cal.App.3d 366, 371 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810875/thorne-v-raccina/)
  Known gap: This is the actual text of Thorne v. Raccina (2012) 203 Cal.App.4th 492, 501, fetched directly from CourtListener (opinion_id 5666330, a lead opinion whose id differs from the cluster id 5810875) and confirmed as an exact substring of the fetched html_with_citations after stripping HTML tags. This is a Court of Appeal decision applying section 2556, not the statute's own text; it is binding only within its own reasoning and does not itself resolve whether any particular asset was actually litigated and divided in any other case. The “crucial question” phrase quoted here is itself drawn by the Thorne court from an earlier decision, Miller v. Miller (1981) 117 Cal.App.3d 366, 371, which this document cites as it appears quoted with approval in Thorne's own opinion; this document does not independently fetch or verify Miller's original opinion text. Whether a specific asset was “actually litigated and divided” by a specific judgment is inherently a fact-specific inquiry turning on the wording of that particular judgment or marital settlement agreement, as Thorne itself illustrates by contrasting the judgment before it with the judgments in Melton and Simundza, two other cases the opinion discusses; this document does not assess that question for any specific judgment.

HISTORICAL BACKGROUND: TENANCY IN COMMON PENDING ADJUDICATION, BEFORE CONTINUING JURISDICTION EXISTED BY STATUTE
Before Family Code section 2556 was enacted, the California Supreme Court addressed the same underlying problem — a community property asset a divorce decree did not adjudicate — in Henn v. Henn. The court there described the settled principle that property which is not mentioned in the pleadings as community property is left unadjudicated by decree of divorce, and is subject to future litigation, the parties being tenants in common meanwhile. At that time, however, the court in Henn also observed that the Legislature had not provided courts of dissolution with continuing jurisdiction to modify a judgment dividing community property after it has become final, which is why the case before it proceeded as a separate civil action rather than as a motion in the original family law case.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "property which is not mentioned in the pleadings as community property is left unadjudicated by decree of divorce, and is subject to future litigation, the parties being tenants in common meanwhile"
  — Henn v. Henn, 26 Cal.3d 323, 330-331 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1356599/henn-v-henn/)
  "The Legislature has not provided courts of dissolution with continuing jurisdiction to modify a judgment dividing community property after it has become final."
  — Henn v. Henn, 26 Cal.3d 323, 332, fn. 7 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1356599/henn-v-henn/)
  Known gap: This is the actual text of Henn v. Henn (1980) 26 Cal.3d 323, fetched directly from CourtListener (a combined opinion whose opinion_id and cluster_id both equal 1356599) and confirmed as an exact substring of the fetched html_with_citations after stripping HTML tags. The first quoted passage is itself a nested quotation: Henn quotes In re Marriage of Brown (1976) 15 Cal.3d 838, 850-851, which in turn quotes In re Marriage of Elkins (1972) 28 Cal.App.3d 899, 903; this document cites the passage as it appears quoted in Henn's own opinion and does not independently fetch or verify the Brown or Elkins opinions. Henn's procedural holding — that the family court itself lacked continuing jurisdiction to modify a final property judgment, so that a separate civil action was the only available remedy — predates and has been legislatively superseded by Family Code section 2556, enacted roughly thirteen years later, which now allows the same adjudication to proceed by postjudgment motion or order to show cause within the original family law proceeding, as this document's companion clause on the procedural mechanism describes; this clause cites Henn only for its substantive tenancy-in-common principle, not for its now-superseded procedural holding. A California Court of Appeal decision, Thorne v. Raccina, has itself made this same point, describing Henn as reflecting the pre-section-2556 rule that a separate partition action was required; this document's companion clause on what counts as omitted addresses Thorne for a different point and does not restate that observation. This document does not address how, if at all, the tenancy-in-common characterization described in Henn affects rights or remedies as between the parties themselves prior to any court adjudication under section 2556.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT — NOT A COURT FILING
